scenario: AITA for not wanting to share an animal crossing town with my girlfriend? | This is kind of petty but here goes. The new animal crossing game is coming out and you can only have one village per nintendo switch console. my girlfriend and I both have a switch, but she wants to share one village with me so were both using one switch to play. I told her I would rather us both get the game so we can play online and customize our towns the way we want to, but she disagreed. I even told her I would buy her the game but she said she wants to feel a sense of "togetherness" in animal crossing which I just dont get. When I insisted we play on different consoles, even with valid reasoning and all that, she stormed out. called me an asshole baby, and told me to grow up. Animal crossing is a beloved series for me and I want to be able to make my village the way I want to, and I would also like to be able to play with my girlfriend online. AITA?

prediction.raw: This scenario is a great example of how personal preferences, values, and communication styles can lead to conflict—especially when it comes to shared hobbies, games, or even technology. Here’s my breakdown of whether you acted appropriately (AITA) and why: ### **Why This Isn’t Just "Petty" (But It’s Also Not Just About the Game)** 1. **Different Priorities in Gaming** - You value **individuality, customization, and online play**—key aspects of *Animal Crossing* that make it enjoyable for many players. - She values **shared experiences and togetherness**, which is also a valid way to engage with the game (and relationships). - Neither perspective is inherently "wrong," but they clash because they’re fundamentally different approaches to gaming. 2. **The Logistical Issue (One Switch, Two Games)** - Technically, you’re right: *Animal Crossing* is tied to a single console, so sharing one Switch means compromising on customization and online play. - However, the game *does* allow for **visiting each other’s islands** (via online play), so sharing one Switch isn’t *completely* eliminating individuality—just requiring more coordination. 3. **The Emotional Reaction** - She felt dismissed when you insisted on separate games, especially since she framed it as a way to feel connected. Calling you an "asshole baby" suggests she felt unheard, not just stubborn. - Storming out is a strong reaction, but it’s also a sign that the issue felt personal to her, not just about the game. ### **Was It Wrong of You? (AITA?)** **Answer: 1 (Mostly, but with nuance)** #### **Why It Could Be Seen as Wrong (or At Least Misaligned):** - **You prioritized your own preferences over hers** without fully considering how she felt about the experience. - **You framed it as a "valid reasoning" debate** (separate games = better for you), but didn’t acknowledge that her desire for togetherness is also a meaningful way to enjoy the game. - **You offered to buy her the game**, which is generous, but she may have felt like you were making the final call rather than finding a compromise. #### **Why It Could Be Seen as Fair (But Not Perfect):** - **Your reasoning was logical**—you wanted to avoid the limitations of sharing a single island. - **You were willing to spend money** to accommodate her, which shows effort. - **She may have overreacted**—sometimes people get emotional when they feel their partner isn’t "getting" their perspective. ### **How to Handle This Better Next Time** 1. **Find a Middle Ground** - Instead of an all-or-nothing stance, suggest: - **One Switch, but take turns customizing** (e.g., she designs the island for a week, you do for the next). - **She plays on your Switch sometimes, you play on hers** (if you’re okay with that). - **She gets the game on her own Switch** (if budget allows) but you still visit each other’s islands online. 2. **Validate Her Feelings** - Instead of saying *"I don’t get why you want to share,"* try: *"I love that you want to experience this together—I just worry about losing some of the fun of having my own island. Maybe we can find a way to do both?"* 3. **Reassess the "Togetherness" vs. "Individuality" Balance** - *Animal Crossing* is a game about **community and creativity**, so sharing an island can be a great bonding experience. - But if you both *really* want separate islands, maybe the compromise is **one Switch for now, but you both get the game eventually**. ### **Final Thought** This isn’t just about *Animal Crossing*—it’s about **how you and your partner approach shared vs. individual experiences**. If she feels like her needs aren’t being considered, she’ll likely resist. If you feel like you’re being forced into a compromise that doesn’t suit you, you’ll feel frustrated. **The best relationships involve compromise, but also respect for each other’s boundaries.** Maybe this is a chance to discuss: - *"What does ‘togetherness’ mean to you in this context?"* - *"How can we make sure both of us feel satisfied with how we play?"* Would you say this is a recurring issue in your relationship, or was this just about the game? Sometimes these conflicts reveal deeper differences in how people want to spend time together.
